title: Rev. Mark V Garringer Obituary - The Star Press
content: Rev. Mark V Garringer, age 86, Farmland, died Friday October 16, 2026 at home following an extended illness.  Born in Winchester on March 25, 1940, he grew up in the Farmland area and was a part of the last graduating class of Green Township High School – the class of 1958.  Mark furthered his education at Taylor University where he received a B.A. in Bible Literacy.  As a Congregational Christian Pastor, Mark served in ministry for nearly 60 years, pastoring in Randolph and Delaware Counties.  Along with his wife, he served with OMS International for a year in Haiti and at the Greenwood (IN) mission headquarters as Assistant Director of Field Ministries in the mid 1980s.  During his final years of pastoring near Selma, Mark served as Men’s Evening Supervisor at the Muncie Mission; his work there was a ministry he cherished.  As a carpenter, he played an integral role in designing, planning, and building a house in Muncie to sell to support OMS.  He also designed and built four duplexes for seniors in Albany.  Mark had a heart of compassion and while he enjoyed farming and mushroom hunting, his biggest joy was in taking care of people. Survivors include his wife of 65 years, Linda Sue “Susie” (Swingley) Garringer; daughter: Gina Garringer, Farmland; son: Jordan Garringer (wife: Lacie), Albany; brother: Lee Garringer (wife: Joyce), Muncie; grandson: Taylor Garringer, and granddaughter: Audrey Garringer. He is preceded in death by his son, Ralph Aaron Garringer; parents: Verlin & Nellie (Lasley) Garringer; brother: Roy Garringer; and nephews: David Garringer, Sr. and James Lee Garringer. Visitation will be Wednesday October 21, 2026 from 3 until 6 p.m. at Meacham Funeral Service with the funeral ceremony at 6 p.m.  Burial will take place on Thursday at Hopewell Cemetery with graveside services at 3 p.m. Preferred memorials are to the Muncie Mission or The Gideons International; condolences and other expressions of sympathy may be given at www.MeachamFuneralService.com. title: Commonwealth v. Gary Zephir Jr. - City of Norfolk (.gov)
content: NORFOLK, Va. — Gary Zephir Jr., 20, was sentenced on Friday to serve 46 years and five months in prison after a jury convicted him in July of first-degree murder and using a firearm in the death of 20-year-old Isaish Tyrell Dukes in 2025 when Mr. Zephir, with the help of a juvenile co-defendant, set up, robbed, and fatally shot Mr. Dukes during a marijuana transaction. On the morning of Jan. 5, 2025, Mr. Zephir, who was 19 at the time, contacted at least five known marijuana dealers to set up a transaction. After his contacts were unsuccessful, Mr. Zephir asked the juvenile co-defendant, who was 16 at the time, to assist by contacting his marijuana dealers. That afternoon, Mr. Zephir told his co-defendant that he intended to rob whoever was willing to set up a transaction. The juvenile co-defendant contacted Mr. Dukes, the two negotiated a transaction, and they agreed to meet at the three-way intersection of Goochland, Chapel, and Proescher streets near Huntersville Park. The co-defendant and Mr. Zephir went to the intersection separately, both armed with handguns. Mr. Dukes drove to the intersection with his friend, who was in the front passenger seat. When they arrived, Mr. Zephir approached the driver’s window, and the juvenile co-defendant stood near the rear of the car. Mr. Zephir greeted Mr. Dukes, complimented the aroma of marijuana coming from Mr. Dukes’s car, and went on to say, "Give me all that right now – if you don't, I’ma blow you." Mr. Zephir then shot Mr. Dukes multiple times at close range, striking him in his head and neck and killing him instantly. Mr. Dukes’s friend testified that he then heard two gunshots, saw Mr. Dukes slump over, and heard Mr. Zephir ask where the bag of marijuana was, to which he responded he did not know. Mr. Dukes’s friend handed his own backpack (which contained his personal items but did not contain marijuana) to Mr. Zephir, opened the glove box (which was empty), and opened the center console (which contained a firearm). Mr. Zephir demanded the firearm, which Mr. Dukes’s friend handed over, and the two defendants ran away. Witnesses in the area who heard the gunshots called 911, and Norfolk Police responded shortly after the two defendants fled. Mr. Dukes was unresponsive when police arrived, and medics pronounced him dead at the scene. With the help of Mr. Dukes’s family, detectives were able to unlock his cellphone, which was left behind in the car following the robbery, and eventually determine the juvenile co-defendant’s identity. As the murder investigation was progressing, police arrested Mr. Zephir on Feb. 26, 2025, for a number of felonies — including possessing a firearm as a convicted felon and maliciously discharging a firearm from a motor vehicle — relating to a different shooting Mr. Zephir committed on B Avenue in Huntersville. Mr. Zephir was sentenced on those charges on May 8, 2026, and ordered to serve four years in prison. At the time of his arrest for that offense, the police had not yet identified either person involved in the murder of Mr. Dukes. The juvenile co-defendant was arrested in April 2025, and Mr. Zephir was later identified as the individual who effected the robbery and shot Mr. Dukes. The juvenile, who did not know that Mr. Zephir was going to shoot the victim, was initially charged with second-degree murder, armed robbery, using a firearm in the commission of those two felonies, and conspiring to commit robbery causing death. The police conducted further investigations to determine Mr. Zephir’s identity and presented that information to the Commonwealth’s Attorney’s Office, which secured indictments against Mr. Zephir in October 2025 for first-degree murder, armed robbery, using a firearm in the commission of those two felonies, and conspiring to commit robbery causing death. Mr. Zephir pleaded not guilty to his charges and opted to be tried by a jury. The Commonwealth proceeded to trial on the two charges of first-degree murder and using a firearm in the commission of murder. The evidence presented by the Commonwealth at trial included testimony by the juvenile co-defendant and Mr. Dukes’s friend who witnessed the shooting as well as security footage, forensic evidence, cellphone data, and more. After hearing the evidence and arguments between July 14 and 16, 2026, and deliberating for nearly three hours, the jury found Mr. Zephir guilty as charged. Judge Jamilah D. LeCruise, who presided over the trial, set Mr. Zephir’s sentencing hearing on Oct. 16. In August 2026, the now-17-year-old juvenile co-defendant entered an agreement to plead guilty to armed robbery and was committed to the Department of Juvenile Justice as a serious offender, where he will remain until up to the age of 21. The juvenile co-defendant will be subject to a suspended adult prison sentence after his commitment and at that point will have to comply with four years of good behavior and a year of adult supervision. At Mr. Zephir’s sentencing hearing on Friday, the Commonwealth argued for Mr. Zephir to serve 43 years and five months in prison, which was the low-end of Mr. Zephir’s state sentencing guidelines. Mr. Zephir’s guidelines were elevated in part because of his conviction for the February 2025 shooting incident. Mr. Zephir’s defense counsel argued for a sentence within Mr. Zephir’s guidelines. After hearing the arguments and noting Mr. Zephir’s apparent lack of remorse during his trial and sentencing hearing, Judge LeCruise sentenced Mr. Zephir to serve 46 years and five months in prison with six months of post-release supervision and another six years and seven months in prison suspended on the conditions that Mr. Zephir completes five years of supervised probation and uniform good behavior following his release. That sentence will run consecutively to the four years that Mr. Zephir will serve for the February 2025 incident. “Gary Zephir needlessly and heartlessly took the life of the victim in this case. I grieve for the victim’s family and hope that this sentence offers them some closure,” said Commonwealth’s Attorney Ramin Fatehi. “Illegal marijuana transactions remain very dangerous for all parties involved in them, which is why I am heartened that, after many years of Republican intransigence from Glenn Youngkin and his allies, Governor Abigail Spanberger, House Speaker Don Scott, and Senate President Pro Tempore Louise Lucas have finally assembled a framework for the legal sale of marijuana in the Commonwealth. Doing so is a matter of public safety: With a legal market in place, the incentives to deal marijuana in the shadows decrease, and so does the probability of violence. Finally, I will note that Mr. Zephir’s co-defendant — a child at the time of his offense — expressed remorse, tried to make amends, and assisted in the prosecution of Mr. Zephir. Those who help the police and prosecutors get to the truth will receive a benefit. Those who do not will face heavier consequences. My office and I will continue to focus our efforts on the individuals who perpetrate violent crime in our city.” Assistant Commonwealth’s Attorney J. Drew Fairbanks and Senior Assistant Commonwealth’s Attorney Andrew Kolp prosecuted Mr. Zephir and his co-defendant’s cases, and Norfolk Police Detective Ryan B. Davis led the investigation.

title: 2027 Ford Ranger Is Set to Add a New Twin-Turbo 3.0-Liter V-6, Just Like the Bronco - Car and Driver
content: The engine, detuned from duty in the Bronco Raptor, should make 380 horsepower and 440 pound-feet of torque. After Ford upgraded the Bronco for 2027 with a new engine, it’s now the Ranger’s turn. The Bronco Raptor’s twin-turbocharged 3.0-liter V-6 has been detuned and spread across the lower rungs of the Bronco lineup, and now it looks like the Ranger is set to get the same powertrain. As reported by Autoevolution, an order guide shows that the Ranger will replace the optional 2.7-liter V-6 with the new twin-turbo 3.0-liter unit. While the Ranger’s XLT and Lariat trims will still come standard with the 270-hp turbocharged 2.3-liter four-cylinder, the optional twin-turbocharged 2.7-liter V-6 is being replaced. The new 3.0-liter engine will continue to be paired with a 10-speed automatic transmission. Although the order guide doesn’t specify, the twin-turbo 3.0-liter V-6 produces 380 hp and 440 pound-feet of torque in the 2027 Bronco, and we expect to see the same figures for Ford’s mid-size truck. That represents an increase of 65 hp and 40 pound-feet over the 2.7-liter. The base XL model will continue to come exclusively with the inline-four. While the base four-cylinder comes standard with rear-wheel drive, the 3.0-liter will only be offered with four-wheel drive. The order guide reveals a few other minor changes coming to the 2027 Ranger. A variety of new wheels will be offered across the lineup, along with new finishes for the grille on the XLT and Lariat. Just as with the Bronco, the Ranger will replace the Velocity Blue paint color with Neptune Blue and will also ditch the Carbonized Gray paint. Inside, the XL now comes standard with the 12.0-inch screen instead of the current 10.1-inch unit, while dual-zone climate control becomes standard on the XL. The Sandstone interior hue has been canceled, with Ford instead adding a new color called Space Gray. Ford has yet to officially confirm these changes, but we expect confirmation to emerge within the next couple of months. The order guide also doesn’t specify pricing for the 2027 Ranger, but we don’t expect the XL’s $35,445 base price to rise by too much. Upgrading to the 2.7-liter currently costs $7545 on the XLT and $5795 on the Lariat, and we hope that price doesn’t increase by much with the new 3.0-liter V-6. title: Pear VC Raises $333 Million Fund V To Back Founders Before The Market Does - Pulse 2.0
content: Pear VC has closed a $333 million Fund V, bringing the early-stage venture firm’s total assets under management to more than $1.1 billion and giving it additional capital to invest primarily in pre-seed and seed-stage startups. The firm said the majority of Fund V will be allocated to new early-stage investments over roughly two and a half years, with additional capital reserved for follow-on investments in portfolio companies that demonstrate strong growth. Founded in 2013, Pear has built its strategy around identifying founders before their companies become widely known or, in some cases, before the startups themselves formally exist. The firm has previously backed companies including DoorDash, Gusto, Vanta, Guardant Health, Affinity, Listen Labs, and Forus. Pear’s founder discovery efforts include PearX, its flagship program for pre-seed entrepreneurs. The program runs twice per year and accepts fewer than 1% of applicants. More than 6,000 startups applied to the Summer 2026 cohort. According to the firm, approximately 80% of PearX companies later raise institutional seed rounds, with some reaching valuations as much as 10 times Pear’s entry price. The firm also operates Pear Studio, a 14,000-square-foot San Francisco hub where PearX founders work directly with investors. Pear’s platform supports portfolio companies across areas including customer discovery, hiring, fundraising, and go-to-market strategy. Its talent team has helped facilitate more than 300 hires across portfolio companies. Recent Pear-backed companies have also reached significant milestones. Listen Labs entered into a definitive agreement to be acquired by Salesforce, while Forus raised a $150 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation. Gravis Robotics raised a $200 million Series A, Vals AI raised $40 million, Andera raised $37 million, and Phinity Labs reached eight figures in annualized run rate. Alongside the fund closing, Pear promoted Arash Afrakhteh, Ajay Kamat, and Shravan Reddy to General Partner. Afrakhteh focuses on enterprise and B2B investments across AI, machine learning, cloud, and data infrastructure. Kamat invests in consumer, fintech, and healthcare companies. Reddy focuses on AI infrastructure, robotics, and vertical AI. “Our ambition is to be the best in the world at one thing: finding extraordinary founders first, before they become obvious to the rest of the market, and helping them build extraordinary companies from zero. Fund V gives us the right amount of capital to keep doing that with focus, discipline, and the same early-stage conviction that defines Pear.” “Capital is becoming commoditized. Access is not. AI now lets anyone build what once took dozens of engineers. We believe the firms closest to founders at the earliest stages, not just to the financing rounds that follow, will have the advantage. Our job is to build relationships with top founder talent months, if not years, before the rest of the market realizes what they are capable of building.” Mar Hershenson, Founding Managing Partner Of Pear VC “Arash, Ajay, and Shravan each embody what makes Pear special: deep care for founders, exceptional leadership, and a selfless commitment to our community. For us, this is one of the most meaningful milestones in Pear’s history. Thirteen years after starting the firm, we now have a new generation of General Partners who have grown with Pear and will help build what comes next.” Pejman Nozad And Mar Hershenson, Founding Managing Partners Of Pear VC Thank you for visiting Pulse 2.0. title: How Heat’s rotation should look on opening night v. Timberwolves - Hot Hot Hoops
content: We’re just over two days away from the Miami Heat’s season opener against the Minnesota Timberwolves. Rotations in today’s NBA are extremely flexible based on matchups, scheme, game flow and who’s available, among many other factors. It’s difficult to be set on the same nine or 10 guys each night. The good news for the Heat is that most everyone practiced this weekend. So how should the rotation shape out once the 7:30 p.m. EST tip-off arrives on Wednesday? Let’s examine! Skinny: He’s not Giannis or Bam, but Davion Mitchell showed why he is the team’s head of the snake on both ends. Mitchell averaged 8.0 points while dishing out five dimes (to two turnovers) in 18.0 minutes per game with Miami this preseason. He was pushing pace whenever he had the opportunity to, setting up open teammates and creating easy transition looks. Mitchell’s motor was a 12 out of 10 on both ends, which ies exactly what you want to see from the 6-foot-1 guard. Skinny: Thompson didn’t shoot the ball well this preseason, going just 3-of-20 from 3-point range. Historically, he’s a “slow” starter, as he’s a career 37.6 percent 3-point shooter over his team’s first 10 games of a new season (41.3 percent otherwise). Those are still very good numbers. The best part was Thompson defended well. Eventually, he’ll find that balance. Skinny: Wiggins was the Heat’s second-leading scorer this preseason, averaging 14.3 points on 60.6 percent shooting and 46.7 percent from deep on 3.8 attempts. Offensively, Wiggins’ role look simplified — and that’s when he’s at his best. As long as he’s burying open threes and holding his ground against the opposing team’s best wing, he’ll be a critical piece to this team. Skinny: Duh! When you’re the only person to ever record 20-15-9 in less than 25 minutes in an NBA game, you’re ready for the season to start. Skinny: Another duh, even though Adebayo is dealing with a groin injury. He practiced on Sunday, though. Bam Adebayo (groin) back at practice today for Heat. Team says everyone did something at practice. Opener Wednesday vs. visiting Timberwolves. Skinny: While Larsson was inactive for three of the Heat’s final four preseason games with an undisclosed illness, I am expecting (not a report) 6-foot-5 guard to be active ahead of Wednesday’s season opener. Larsson is the quintessential glue guy that should blossom alongside Antetokounmpo and Adebayo, although he will begin the season in the Heat’s second unit. Skinny: Hardaway, who finished third in Sixth Man of the Year voting last year, didn’t miss a beat. He averaged 11.5 points on 42.1 percent shooting from distance in preseason. There’s always going to be pressure when you’re wearing your father’s number, but I think Hardaway will acclimate himself just fine as a movement shooter and spot-up threat. Skinny: Portis functions as an extra big behind Adebayo and Antetokounmpo. He’s a good rebounder and 3-point shooter, shooting 40.0 percent on 3.8 triple tries across four preseason games. Should he carry that efficiency over, Portis will be one of the most impactful bigs in an Eastern Conference that lacks big depth. Skinny: Jovic, 23, did everything that was asked of him this preseason to earn a rotation spot. He shot the ball well (led the team in 3P%), sported a 3.6 assist-to-turnover ratio and defended at an above-average level. I was also impressed with his slashing and his finishing through contact, which can still be hit-and-miss. Now, it’s time for him to carry that over into the regular season on a consistent level. Skinny: Conwell blossomed toward the end of preseason, averaging 18.7 points and 5.7 assists on 40.0 percent shooting from 3-point range over his final three games. His quick-trigger 3-point shooting will be an asset at some point, even if he doesn’t begin the year in the rotation. Skinny: Fontecchio led the team in made 3-pointers (9) during preseason, knocking them down at a 37.8 percent clip, averaging 8.6 points. He’s another body who Erik Spoelstra can trust to provide some extra spacing and knock down shots, specifically alongside Antetokounmpo. Skinny: I still view Richards as more of an insurance big than a rotational big man. But he was the Heat’s leading rebounder in five games, grabbing 8.4 boards with a 31.7 defensive rebound percentage and a 20.9 total rebound percentage. Those are numbers you ultimately can’t ignore. He knows his role. Minnesota will be a very tough challenge for Miami coming out the gate. The T’Wolves added Ball and Kuminga to an already strong group. title: NFL today: How to watch Commanders v 49ers, TV channels & live stream Monday 19 October - The Guardian
content: How will the Commanders and 49ers fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options The Commanders’ first task on Monday night against the 49ers will be to keep track of the clock. A week after frittering away a simple game-winning field goal opportunity in overtime against the Giants, Washington’s reward is a trip out west on Monday Night Football to face one of the best teams in the NFL. The 1-3-1 Commanders entered the week with the second-worst point differential in the NFC at minus-34, and it’ll take a herculean road effort for them to avoid falling out of the mix in the mediocre East. The Niners, meanwhile, are on Easy Street. Their 5-0 start has afforded them a shocking degree of cushion in an NFC West that was expected to be the best division in football but so far looks like San Francisco and everyone else. The defending champion Seahawks and MVP Matthew Stafford’s Rams each dropped three games in the season’s first six weeks. Those included a pair of losses to Kyle Shanahan’s team, meaning the Niners have not just a huge advantage in the loss column but (for now) a head-to-head tiebreaker as well. San Fran could hardly have enjoyed a dreamier start. And yet! The NFL has a way of pulling everybody back toward the middle, so perhaps the world should be on alert for something shocking to happen when the Commanders arrive in Santa Clara. United States: Watch on ESPN or ABC, or stream on the ESPN app or Fubo (with ESPN or the local ABC affiliate). Canada: Watch on TSN1/3/4 or CTV2 (RDS2 in French), or stream on DAZN or Fubo Sports Pro. United Kingdom: Watch on Sky Sports NFL or Sky Sports Main Event, or stream with NOW or NFL Game Pass on DAZN. The Commanders have lots of problems to confront this week, but one of them is new. The bright spot of their tough start has been a robust running game, which ranked fifth in the league in yardage (698) entering the week. The top man in that attack has been second-year tailback Jacory Croskey-Merritt, who carried 11 times for 82 yards in the team’s debacle of a tie against the Giants last week. But Croskey-Merritt is out this week with a groin injury, meaning a heavy running load will shift to QB Jayden Daniels and a veteran running back duo of Austin Ekeler and Rachaad White. Will the Commanders be able to keep up a 4.7-yard rushing average without their lead back? The 49ers don’t have “problems” these days. The absence of star edge rusher Nick Bosa would have been one, but the 49ers just sacked Sam Darnold five times without him, and Bosa is expected to return from his late-September calf strain for this game. Brock Purdy is playing the best football of his career, and somehow his offensive supporting cast of senior citizens – the very old Christian McCaffrey, George Kittle, Mike Evans, and Trent Williams – continues to be timelessly great. The defense has been more average than terrific, but you’d expect it to get better as it gets healthier. One subplot to watch will be how quickly Bosa gets back to looking like Bosa, assuming he makes his third start of the year.

title: The Supreme Court’s Right Flank Wants to Give You Fewer Privacy Rights Than a Famous Judge - Balls and Strikes
content: Want more Balls & Strikes? Sign up for our free newsletter here. This story was published in partnership with Slate. In 2022, college sports fan Michael Salazar became a digital subscriber to 247Sports.com, a website that shares news about NCAA football and basketball. In order to register for the website, owned by Paramount Global, Salazar signed up for 247Sports’ online newsletter. And he used his subscription to view sports-related video media. Quietly embedded within those videos, though, was a tracking pixel created by Facebook. Because Paramount installed Facebook’s tracking pixel on the 247Sports website, every time Salazar requested or viewed a video, Paramount automatically disclosed the name and URL of the video to Facebook, along with Salazar’s Facebook ID, the unique identifier Facebook assigns to all of its users. Facebook then used that information to show Salazar targeted advertisements. Privacy violations like this have become a routine part of life on the internet. According to a 2024 study on website privacy, more than half of all companies listed in the S&P 500 index use the “Meta pixel” on their sites, sharing people’s information with both Facebook and Instagram. But in theory, there are at least some legal boundaries. Back in 1988, after a D.C. journalist obtained and published a list of movies rented by Supreme Court nominee Robert Bork, a scandalized Congress passed the Video Privacy Protection Act. To be clear: Congress was scandalized by the nonconsensual disclosure of Bork’s rental history, not the judge’s viewing habits, which were pretty unremarkable (unlike those of another judicial nominee who would be confirmed to the Supreme Court a few years later.) The VPPA prohibits videotape service providers from knowingly disclosing the personally identifiable information of consumers, unless they get the consumers’ written consent. The statute defines “videotape service provider” to include any person in the business of delivering “prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials.” And the definition of “consumer” includes any “subscriber of goods or services” from the provider. Here, Salazar subscribed to Paramount’s sports website. He requested audiovisual materials from Paramount, and Paramount delivered them. And then Paramount knowingly disclosed what he watched to Facebook without getting his consent. In September 2022, Salazar filed a class-action lawsuit, arguing that Paramount violated the VPPA. But in July 2023, the federal district court dismissed his complaint, reasoning that Salazar didn’t count as a “consumer” under the statute because he was only subscribed to a newsletter, “not audio visual content.” Salazar appealed to the 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, but in April 2025, a divided three-judge panel affirmed the dismissal, agreeing with the district court that Salazar’s newsletter subscription didn’t make him a subscriber under the law. Then Salazar appealed to the Supreme Court, which heard oral arguments in Salazar v. Paramount on Wednesday. Under the plain text of the Video Privacy Protection Act, Salazar should be able to hold Paramount liable for its disclosure of his video history. But during the oral arguments, the Republican-nominated justices peppered Salazar’s attorney with questions suggesting that imposing an atextual limitation onto the statute—one that would conveniently insulate corporations from legal liability when they intrude on consumers’ privacy for profit—was really just the commonsense thing to do. “Wouldn’t it be natural to think that goods or services from a videotape service provider would be video-related services?” asked Justice Clarence Thomas. Later in the oral argument, Thomas said he “always thought of 247Sports as a sports site,” and he questioned the “logic” of viewing the site as a “videotape service provider.” Justice Samuel Alito further argued that the law was “based on the technology of the 1980s,” when people had to “go to a Blockbuster store and get a VHS tape.” Although the text of the VPPA appears to cover Salazar’s claims, Alito suggested that a newsletter subscription isn’t analogous enough to what Congress had in mind and asked Salazar’s counsel why he thought the “smart lower court judges” who ruled against him rejected his “very literal interpretation” of the statute. Justice Brett Kavanaugh echoed these concerns: “We are a textualist Court but usually not a literalist Court,” he said. Kavanaugh continued, “Congress in the 1980s wasn’t thinking about data sharing for targeted advertising.” Kavanaugh and Justice Amy Coney Barrett also worried that, if the VPPA weren’t limited to the long-defunct Blockbusters of the world, practically any business could find themselves liable under the law. Kavanaugh brought up concerns, raised by corporate interest groups in amicus briefs, that “every business in America that has video on its website” could be targeted. Trying to suss out the scope of the statute, Kavanaugh and Barrett both asked how long a video must be for a company to count as a video service provider. Salazar’s attorney indicated that length wasn’t especially relevant and shifted the conversation to the business and profit motive of delivering videos, but Barrett was skeptical. “If I’m on Nordstrom’s website and I click to see the model show me what the shoes are going to look like,” said Barrett, “that’s a profit motive.” For all the Republican justices’ stated concern on Wednesday about reading and interpreting the VPPA in a way that makes sense, they failed to meaningfully engage with the text and context. Paramount provided Salazar with videos and then told Facebook what videos he watched without his consent—the exact kind of injury contemplated by the statute. Technology and commerce have obviously changed considerably since Congress passed the Video Privacy Protection Act. But the law’s commitment to protecting the privacy of video consumers has not. What has changed, however, is the ideological commitments of the people who sit on the court. title: Betts v. Boone County Brief: Coroner Trophy-Skull Case Merits Supreme Court Review - Cato Institute
content: Sign up to have blog posts delivered straight to your inbox! Decades ago, the Supreme Court held in a case called Monell v. Department of Social Services that you can sue a local government for violating your constitutional rights only if the violation resulted from the locale’s “official policy.” In other words, if a county employee goes rogue, you can’t hold the county itself responsible. A new court decision stretches Monell to the point of absurdity, holding that the county’s top official does not set official county policy. Boone County, Illinois’s coroner, Wesley Hyland, committed a constitutional violation of an uncommonly disturbing sort. He “kept several skulls as trophies from the deceased he examined,” according to the Seventh Circuit. One of them belonged to a high school student who was kidnapped, raped, and murdered. Forty-five years later, her brothers learned that Hyland had held onto her skull. They recovered it, exhumed her other remains, and reburied them together. Then, they sued Boone County. So in spite of his role as coroner, he “frustrated” official policy rather than deciding it. That means Boone County bears no responsibility for his acts—even though Hyland was Boone County’s decision-maker concerning the treatment of remains. If the girl’s family lived in the Third, Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, Tenth, or Eleventh Circuits, they could recover from their local government under Section 1983. But because they live in the Seventh Circuit, they cannot. Cato, assisted by the University of Virginia School of Law Supreme Court Litigation Clinic and joined by the Due Process Institute, Public Accountability, and the Rutherford Institute, filed an amicus brief asking the Supreme Court to reverse the Seventh Circuit’s decision. The ability to pursue compensation—under federal statute—for violations of federal constitutional rights should not vary by state. title: DC All In Saga: The New Gods by Ram V, Alex Paknadel and Joan Urgell - Bleeding Cool News
content: DC All In Saga: The New Gods by Ram V, Alex Paknadel and Joan Urgell launches in 2027 The Fourth World is coming to Earth, and Mister Miracle is the one stuck holding the keys. DC Comics announced today that DC All In Saga: The New Gods #1, a 48-page one-shot by writers Ram V and Alex Paknadel with art by Joan Urgell, will arrive on the 13th of January, 2027. The book brings Scott Free and the surviving New Gods directly into the unfolding DC All In Saga. Becoming Highfather on a hostile Earth may be the one trap he can't break free from. "Mister Miracle thought he could escape anything. But in the wake of unimaginable upheaval, Scott Free has taken on a role he can't escape: Highfather. With New Genesis occupied by sinister alien forces, the New Gods have taken refuge on Earth, leaving Scott responsible for leading a displaced people searching for safety on a planet that is not their own Their arrival on our world will not go unnoticed. Fourth World technology is being illegally traded on Earth, and tensions are rising as Mister Miracle and the New Gods attempt to peacefully coexist with their new neighbors. With their homeworld beyond their reach and their extraordinary technology falling into dangerous hands, the remaining New Gods must find their place in the DC Universe before the fragile sanctuary they have found becomes another battlefield." The one-shot builds on the larger story that began in 2024's DC All In Special #1 and continues this month in DC All In Saga: Darkseid vs. The World #1 by Scott Snyder, Joshua Williamson, Sanford Greene, and Yasmine Putri, and was also teased in Justice League Unlimited and Justice League Quarterly. Darkseid's shadow has hung over the entire All In initiative from the start, and even as the surviving New Gods face their own crisis, that shadow remains impossible to escape. "I've been itching to get back to The New Gods," said Ram V, who previously wrote the 12-issue The New Gods series with Evan Cagle. "With this one-shot, it was an opportunity to dive back in, check in on where we left them and what they've been up to, and perhaps set up a few things for exciting new New Gods stories to come. As the All In Saga brings the greater story of the DC Universe to a pivotal point, the New Gods must make an important decision about their future, one that will define not only their destinies, but those of the humans and superhumans they've come to call friends." Talking of friends, It's time to make some White Noise. "It's exciting to be working with Alex Paknadel, who's a friend and an incredible co-writer, and with Joan Urgell, whose work is sure to be a treat for readers!" The main cover is by Nimit Malavia, with variant covers by Dustin Nguyen, Kyuyong Eom, Jason Shawn Alexander, and Javi Fernández (plus a foil variant by Nguyen). Colours by Romulo Fajardo, Jr. 48-pages, $5.99 ($6.99 for card-stock).

title: Consumers' Research v. FCC: The Fifth Circuit Rules Again - Benton Institute for Broadband & Society
content:
On October 15, 2026, a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit held that the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) broke a 1945 federal law when it created the Universal Service Administrative Company (USAC), the private, not-for-profit corporation that runs the day-to-day operations of the Universal Service Fund (USF).1 Because the FCC relied on USAC's projections to set what telecommunications carriers owed the USF for the fourth quarter of 2025, the court vacated (that is, canceled) that quarter's "contribution factor" and returned the matter to the FCC. The stakes reach well beyond one quarter's bill for the USF. The fund pays for four programs: Lifeline (discounted phone service for low-income consumers), High Cost (support for carriers serving rural, insular, and other high-cost areas), E-Rate (discounts for schools and libraries), and Rural Health Care (support for rural hospitals and clinics). USAC bills and collects carrier contributions, distributes the money to program beneficiaries, and its directors sit on committees with "authority to make decisions concerning" the programs' operation. The court's core holding is that USAC itself was established unlawfully—not merely that one calculation was flawed. The ruling arrives 16 months after the same lead challenger, Consumers' Research, lost at the U.S. Supreme Court. On June 27, 2025, in FCC v. Consumers' Research, the Supreme Court held 6–3 that Section 254 of the Communications Act, the statute underlying the USF, does not unconstitutionally delegate Congress's legislative power to the FCC. As Benton Senior Counselor Andrew Jay Schwartzman explained at the time, the Supreme Court also rejected the argument that the FCC unconstitutionally handed power to USAC, finding that the FCC exercises firm control over USAC's functions. The new case shifts the attack from the Constitution to a statute: the Government Corporation Control Act (GCCA). The FCC did not defend USAC alone. Several organizations intervened (that is, formally joined the case) in support of the FCC. Among them were the Schools, Health & Libraries Broadband (SHLB) Coalition, which presented oral argument; the National Telecommunications Cooperative Association (NTCA); and the Benton Institute for Broadband & Society, together with the National Digital Inclusion Alliance and MediaJustice. NTCA's role was significant: it presented its own defenses on the GCCA question, including at least one the FCC did not make, and the court addressed each of NTCA's arguments. Consumers' Research challenged a single number: the USF contribution factor for October–December 2025. That factor is a percentage. Its numerator is the USF's projected expenses for the coming quarter; its denominator is the projected revenue of contributing carriers. Each carrier pays its own projected revenue times the factor and may pass that cost on to customers. USAC prepares both projections and submits them to the FCC for approval. In August 2025, USAC projected $2.25 billion in USF expenses and program demand for the quarter. The petitioners—Consumers' Research (described by the court as "a nonprofit organization that aims to educate consumers"), Cause Based Commerce, Inc. (a reseller of telecommunications services that pays directly into the USF), and several individual consumers—filed comments at the FCC arguing that various aspects of the USF are unlawful. They asked the FCC to set the factor at 0.0%, or at least to reduce it to strip out "any unlawful portions."  They filed a second comment making the same arguments on the day the FCC proposed the factor. In court, the petitioners raised four legal theories. The court reached and decided only one: that the FCC created USAC without the specific congressional authorization the GCCA requires, so the FCC could not lawfully rely on USAC to set the factor.2 Initially, the FCC answered by not answering. The FCC issued a public notice proposing a fourth-quarter 2025 factor of 38.1 percent. The agency largely adopted USAC's projections, with one change: the FCC directed USAC to apply $100 million in unused E-Rate funds to offset $628.68 million in projected E-Rate demand, lowering the factor below what USAC's filings alone would have produced. The FCC took no action on the petitioners' comments, and under FCC rules the proposed factor was "deemed approved" 14 days later. In court, the FCC and the intervenors defended USAC on three fronts. According to the opinion, two of the arguments came from NTCA alone. Notably, the opinion reports that "the parties do not contest that the FCC established USAC." The fight was over whether USAC was established "to act as an agency" and whether Congress authorized it. The court granted the petition, vacated the fourth-quarter 2025 contribution factor, and remanded (sent back) to the FCC "for further proceedings." The reasoning moved in five steps. 1. The case could be heard. Cause Based Commerce had standing because it paid directly into the USF—"a classic pocketbook injury." The case was not moot even though the quarter had passed, because quarterly factors are "capable of repetition, yet evading review."  On timeliness, the court rejected NTCA's Hobbs Act argument: each time the FCC uses USAC's projections to set a new factor, it "effectively reapplies" its decision establishing USAC, which "restarts the sixty-day clock." The petition was filed two days after the factor was deemed approved. 2. The GCCA applies to USAC. The GCCA, enacted in 1945 after government-created corporations "had gotten out of hand," provides that an "agency may establish or acquire a corporation to act as an agency only by or under a law of the United States specifically authorizing the action."  The court found the FCC "established" USAC: in 1997 the FCC directed NECA—an entity the FCC itself created in 1983—to form USAC and approved its Delaware incorporation papers. The court then read "to act as an agency" to include acting as an "instrumentality" of the government, relying on the GCCA's original 1945 wording and the 1982 recodification's statement that it made no substantive change. USAC qualifies because the FCC created it to administer the USF "in a manner accountable to the FCC," and because the FCC–USAC Memorandum of Understanding of October 17, 2024 describes USAC's "sole purpose" as assisting the FCC "as an agent and instrumentality of the FCC." 3. The "advisory role" defense failed. Even when only making recommendations, the court said, USAC is the FCC's "means" of calculating the factor. The Supreme Court's approval of agency reliance on private advice addressed the Constitution; reliance on a corporation the agency itself created "can still run afoul of the GCCA." 4. Congress never specifically authorized USAC. The court rejected each claimed source of authority: 5. Vacatur, not remand alone. Vacatur is a court order that sets aside an agency action so it no longer has legal effect. In the Fifth Circuit, vacatur is the default remedy for unlawful agency action; a court departs from it only if there is a "serious possibility" the agency can fix the defect on remand and vacatur would be disruptive. Because the FCC adopted USAC's projections "in toto" (in full) with one adjustment, the court called reliance on USAC a "serious procedural" deficiency the FCC "would not be able to correct on remand." In a footnote, the court acknowledged that whether the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) authorizes courts to vacate agency action at all "has come under scrutiny," citing Justice Gorsuch and the Supreme Court's 2025 decision in Trump v. CASA, but said it remains bound by circuit precedent. The FCC has several paths, and they can be combined. As of October 19, 2026, the FCC has made no public statement about which it will take. 1. Ask the Fifth Circuit to reconsider. The FCC can petition the same three-judge panel for rehearing, or ask the full Fifth Circuit to rehear the case en banc. Because a federal agency is a party, the deadline is 45 days after judgment rather than the usual 14. En banc rehearing "is not favored" and is ordinarily granted only for conflicts with other decisions or "questions of exceptional importance." 2. Ask the Supreme Court to review. A petition for a writ of certiorari (a request that the Supreme Court hear the case, which it may decline) is due within 90 days of the judgment (about January 13, 2027), but a timely rehearing petition resets that clock to run from the date rehearing is denied. A CommLaw Group advisory notes there is no direct split among the federal appeals courts on this question, while suggesting the decision's nationwide consequences could independently attract the Court's interest. 3. Seek to delay the ruling's effect. The Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure govern when the court's "mandate" issues—the formal step that makes the judgment effective—and allow a party to ask that it be stayed. 4. Respond on remand. The court sent the matter back "for further proceedings" but did not say what those proceedings should be. The court also said the FCC "would not be able to correct" its reliance on USAC on remand. The opinion does not say whether the FCC could recalculate the fourth-quarter 2025 factor without USAC, and it does not address refunds. The CommLaw Group advisory likewise notes that the court "did not order refunds or establish a process for recovering previously paid contributions." 5. Ask Congress for specific authorization. The GCCA permits an agency-created corporation "by or under a law of the United States specifically authorizing the action." Legislation specifically authorizing USAC is therefore one path. The ruling vacates only the fourth-quarter 2025 factor. The CommLaw Group advisory says other quarters' factors, including the fourth-quarter 2026 factor of 42.0 percent, "were not directly adjudicated," meaning the court did not rule on them. The advisory also tells carriers not to stop paying contributions or collecting customer surcharges based on this decision. But the court's timeliness reasoning—that every new factor "restarts the sixty-day clock"—invites a fresh challenge each quarter. Consumers' Research has also challenged each quarterly factor the FCC has set since the Supreme Court's decision, in Fifth Circuit Nos. 26-60003, 26-60214, 26-60511, and 26-60863. The first three have been held in abeyance (paused) awaiting last week's decision. If the court applies the same reasoning, those quarterly factors would fall as well. It is too early to assess the decision's practical effect. But the coming months are likely to bring considerable uncertainty about how a multibillion-dollar program will operate going forward. title: 2028 Honda CR-V - Yahoo Autos
content: Honda's compact SUV, the CR-V, has built its reputation on roomy practicality, easy-to-use controls, and a comfortable drive. The seventh-generation model is expected to keep that family-friendly formula, but make hybrid power central to the lineup, with a new system and electric all-wheel drive potentially improving efficiency and traction. Compact SUV competitors include the Toyota RAV4, Hyundai Tucson Hybrid, and Subaru Forester Hybrid. The redesigned 2028 CR-V is expected to receive a next-generation hybrid system as Honda begins rolling out its new "Honda Hybrid" technology globally in 2027. Honda says the system builds on its existing two-motor setup, with efficiency improvements to the engine and drive unit. Honda is also developing a new electric all-wheel-drive system for its next-generation hybrids. It uses a rear electric motor, unlike the outgoing CR-V Hybrid's mechanical AWD system. The seventh-generation CR-V arrives for spring 2027. This page will be updated with more insights and photos as information becomes available. The CR-V has long balanced a spacious interior with a pleasant driving experience and controls that are easy to use. Its next-generation hybrid system could improve fuel economy and driving refinement, and a new AWD setup with a rear electric motor may deliver smoother, more responsive traction than the outgoing model's mechanical system. We expect the TrailSport to return as well, and hope its cabin feels more distinctive than the outgoing SUV's. The 2028 CR-V is expected to go hybrid-only, likely with Honda's next-generation "Honda Hybrid" system. Set to begin rolling out globally in 2027, it builds on the automaker's existing two-motor setup, with improvements to engine and drive-unit efficiency. Honda hasn't shared CR-V-specific details, but the changes could help the SUV improve on the current hybrid's fuel economy, which trails the Toyota RAV4 Hybrid in most configurations. The outgoing CR-V Hybrid uses a 2.0-liter naturally aspirated four-cylinder. Honda could switch to a version of its 1.5-liter turbocharged engine, though that remains speculation. We hope any powertrain changes preserve the CR-V's choice of front- or all-wheel drive, and that the redesigned model can approach 600 miles of driving range. It should also improve on fuel economy, which is 43/36 mpg city/highway for the 2027 model with FWD and 40/34 mpg with AWD, with the TrailSport getting slightly worse. We wouldn't say no to more grunt, either. The outgoing CR-V Hybrid makes 204 hp and 247 lb-ft of torque, enabling acceleration to 60 mph in a MotorTrend-tested 7.4 seconds. Getting that time down with a little more output would make the SUV even more competitive. Honda Sensing will almost certainly be included with the next CR-V. Driver-assist systems should include: Automatic emergency braking and forward collision warning When Honda launched the sixth-generation CR-V, it pushed the boundaries of the compact segment by adding a significant 2.7 inches in length and 1.6 inches to the wheelbase. Having achieved this mature, commanding road presence, Honda may have hit a physical ceiling. Early prototype spy shots confirm that the upcoming 2028 model will break the historic cycle of dimensional bloat, keeping its overall exterior footprint and proportions virtually identical to the model it replaces. The next CR-V should still be a five-seater. For some context, dimensions for the outgoing model include: Cargo Capacity (seats up/seats down): 39.3/76.5 cubic feet The outgoing CR-V's 9.0-inch touchscreen could carry over on lower trims, but we hope Honda makes the Accord's larger 12.3-inch display standard on most models. The redesigned SUV should also bring updated adaptive cruise control and lane-centering technology, along with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, and a wireless phone charger. Honda could add its Prelude-derived Sport+ drive mode to top-trim Sport Touring models, simulating gear changes for a more engaging feel. We've tested the feature in the Prelude and haven't been convinced; we'd rather see ventilated front seats and a 360-degree camera, features Honda already offers on the outgoing CR-V in other markets. The last CR-V TrailSport paired its hybrid powertrain with standard all-wheel drive, all-terrain tires, and more ground clearance than the standard CR-V: 8.2 inches versus 7.8. If the redesigned CR-V goes hybrid-only, the next TrailSport will certainly keep that setup, a sensible match for the trim's mild off-road ambitions. Model-specific exterior and interior details helped set it apart, and orange ambient lighting, rubber all-season floor mats, a heated steering wheel, and heated front seats added a few practical comforts. We expect the next TrailSport to carry on that formula.

title: Jacob Tierney on the Secrets and Sudden Success of ‘Heated Rivalry’ - V Magazine
content: In his new book, I’ll Believe In Anything, the Heated Rivalry showrunner goes behind the scenes of a romance built on bro-ey masculinity, body language, and bold creative choices In his new book, I’ll Believe In Anything, the Heated Rivalry showrunner goes behind the scenes of a romance built on bro-ey masculinity, body language, and bold creative choices For most of the past year, the internet has been studying two hockey players’ butts and bodies on screens big and small. Lead actors Connor Storrie (as Ilya Rozanov) and Hudson Williams (as Shane Hollander) starred in some of the most-watched queer sex scenes of all time, and Jacob Tierney, the showrunner behind Heated Rivalry, made sure we could see everything the right way. The last time I spoke with him, the TV show hadn’t even premiered yet. It has since received a Peabody, a shelf full of Canadian Screen Awards, and a season-two renewal. Tierney’s new book, I’ll Believe in Anything: The Making of Heated Rivalry Season 1, is a collection of annotated scripts that reveal candid details about adapting Rachel Reid’s Game Changers series of novels to TV. The books treat sex as a character — Shane folding his clothes, Ilya’s gaze commanding a room — and so does the showrunner. “Body language is everything. Every line they say to each other until episode five is bullshit,” Tierney tells VMAN. “You have to see what they’re doing, because everything that comes out of their mouth is obfuscation. That was something we were very aware of. It’s very bro-ey, very masculine, very hockey.” He adds, “It’s not like they can’t find another guy with a great body or whatever. So this physical connection isn’t just shallow. What they reveal about themselves when they’re together, when they’re not talking, is absolutely the whole relationship.” Body language is also how gaydars beep, and how queer men cruise. “Ilya is endlessly cruising,” Tierney says. “Ilya is the one looking for connection. Ilya is a beacon. Every queer hockey player comes to Ilya. At some point, they find him, or he finds them,” within the Game Changers universe. Comparatively, Scott Hunter (François Arnaud) is the total opposite. “Scott is so afraid that his gaydar is shut off. He doesn’t want to know if anybody is gay,” Tierney teases. “Scott is in full Ken-doll, big-brother mode, you know? ‘Hi, how are you? I am Scott, I am Captain America.’” Scott and Kip (Robbie G.K.) get episode three to themselves, then a cathartic kiss on the ice rink in episode five, which has even straight men crying during watch parties. How did Tierney navigate the risk of audiences rejecting this other couple entering the narrative? Or perhaps even liking them too much, over the actual protagonists? “I knew that we were doing something structurally different with this…But I liked the idea of devoting this time to them. I thought it was cleaner,” Tierney reflects. “François freaked out. [Laughs.] He called me, and he was like, ‘The show is doing really well. They’re going to hate me!’…I was like, ‘I don’t think they will!’” Despite the show’s budget constraints, no resources are spared in preparation for the sex scenes in Heated Rivalry, which are shot as long takes with minimal coverage. “You have to do that so the audience feels permission to observe them,” Tierney says. “Seeing how one of them backs away a bit, and the other one comes forward, it tells you everything you need to know about that moment.” This makes rewatching the scenes much more interesting, too. “Watch Ilya this time,” he muses. “Next time, watch Shane.” Tierney is equally thoughtful when asked about Storrie and Williams’s naked bodies going instantly viral amid the two-episode premiere of Heated Rivalry. “The care I take is with Connor and Hudson,” he remarks. “Those are my friends. Those are my wards. I owe them a lot. We’re intertwined. Their wellbeing and safety are very important to me.” “We just had our intimacy rehearsals for season two,” he adds. “We went through all the stuff that we’re going to go through again, and we try to make sure that they’re really comfortable. They’re still so close, and they’re so game. They love these roles. They love doing it. They understood, from day one, that this is important.” Tierney admits, “I try to be very conscious that it hasn’t even been a year since this show’s been out, and they’re arguably two of the most famous people in the world. It’s fucking crazy, and there’s nothing that can prepare you for that. There’s no handbook to it. So, we just check in a lot. ‘You good?’ ‘You need anything?’” So when did he clock the scale of the Heated Rivalry phenomenon? “The HBO Golden Globes party in LA,” Tierney says. “Brendan [Brady] and I were there before Connor and Hudson arrived. And then they did, and I was like, ‘Are they the most famous people here?’” He recalls seeing a “very famous movie star awkwardly trying to figure out how to come over, and what to say.” His takeaway? “This is fucking nuts.” I’ll Believe in Anything: The Making of Heated Rivalry Season 1 is out now from Little, Brown and Company. Season two of Heated Rivalry is expected to premiere in Spring 2027. Rachel Reid’s final novel about Ilya and Shane, Unrivaled, is set for release on June 1, 2027. title: Kistos brings Balder Phase V, King wells online as Q3 output hits 18,500 boed - World Oil
content:
(WO) – Kistos’ pro forma production averaged about 18,500 boed in the third quarter, down from 20,800 boed in the first half, while the Jotun FPSO in Norway went through a 26-day planned turnaround in July. Year-to-date production through Sept. 30 averaged about 20,000 boed. The company kept its full-year guidance of 19,000–21,000 boed. In Norway, the last two Balder Phase V wells started up in July. The King well, drilled from the Ringhorne platform, came on stream in August, ahead of schedule. On Oct. 14, Kistos agreed to buy a 10% working interest in PL 169E, PL 956 and PL 956B from Vår Energi for $12.9 million upfront. The deal adds 4.3 MMboe net in combined 2P reserves and 2C resources and still needs approval from Norway’s Ministry of Energy. Uptime was high across the company’s UK and Dutch assets. Year-to-date production efficiency was about 95% in the Greater Laggan Area, now operated by Serica Energy, and 93% at the Q10-A platform in the Dutch North Sea. The annual turnaround at Q10-A finished on schedule and under budget, along with a jacket integrity inspection campaign. In the Greater Laggan Area, the Adura-operated Victory field is raising throughput at the Shetland Gas Plant and lowering unit operating costs. In Oman, Kistos completed its acquisition of Blocks 3 & 4 on Sept. 14. The interest will be consolidated in its results from Oct. 1. Production there is close to plan, supported by new oil from the Safi and AGW areas. Completion of the Block 9 deal is expected in the fourth quarter. The Block 9 operator has added a fifth drilling rig since revised terms under the block’s production-sharing agreement took effect July 1. “Production in the quarter was impacted by the planned turnaround on the Jotun FPSO but, with the final Balder Phase V wells and the King well now on stream, we remain on track to deliver production within our 2026 pro forma guidance range of 19,000–21,000 boepd,” said Executive Chairman Andrew Austin. title: Liam Coen evaluates Travis Hunter's play in Jaguars v. Texans game - Yahoo Sports
content: The outcome on Sunday wasn't what the Jacksonville Jaguars had hoped for, but this latest matchup with the Houston Texans showcased the high-end two-way impact that Travis Hunter can have. Down 10 points in the fourth quarter, Trevor Lawrence connected with Hunter twice, once on a 26-yard gain and then again later on for a 7-yard score. On the ensuring Texans' offensive drive, with Houston about to make it a two-score game, Hunter undercut a throw from CJ Stroud, coming away with the interception in the end zone. Following the game, Liam Coen shared what he saw from Hunter. "[Hunter] made some critical plays for us on both sides of the football," Coen said, via ESPN. "… We've got to continue to get him the ball and keep building off of it and making sure it fits within the rhythm and flow of the game. But he definitely helped put us in a position to win that game today." You could tell that there was a concerted effort to get Hunter more involved on offense in this game. He went on to record a season-high four receptions for 59 yards. Defensively, Hunter continued to shoulder a larger role, playing 62 offensive snaps. He allowed just two receptions on four targets, but did surrender a 42-yard catch to Nico Collins. Hunter was in on four total tackles as well. Perhaps we will continue to see Hunter's role on offense continue to expand moving forward. "Was proud of the way [Hunter] competed," Coen said. "[He] made some plays for us on offense and we've got to keep building off of it." This article originally appeared on Jaguars Wire: Liam Coen evaluates Travis Hunter's play in Jaguars v. title: Despite Galatolo scandal, college district asks voters to approve Measure V, another bond measure - Palo Alto Daily Post
content:
As former chancellor of the San Mateo County Community College District Ron Galatolo awaits his release from jail, his former employer is seeking voter approval for nearly a billion dollars in construction projects. Measure V asks voters to authorize $848 million in bonds for the San Mateo County Community College District for a new gym, upgrades to two arts buildings and a slew of other repairs at the district’s three campuses: Canada College in Redwood City, College of San Mateo and Skyline College in San Bruno. District officials are planning to spend a chunk of the bond at Skyline, which has not gotten the same facelifts as the other two colleges, which were the beneficiaries of bond measures in 2014 and 2005. Those bond measures also led to trouble for Galatolo, who is currently serving an eight-month jail sentence in Maple Street Jail in Redwood City. He was sentenced in July after being convicted of lying about receiving lavish gifts from contractors and in return gave the firms expensive contracts paid for by the previous bond measures. He will be released on Nov. 27. The bond measure needs to get 55% of the vote to pass. If approved, Measure V would extend an existing property tax levy of $18 per $100,000 of a home’s assessed value. The owner of a $2.15 million home in San Mateo County — the county’s median home price — would pay $386 per year. The levy would raise approximately $75 million annually for construction projects. Including interest, taxpayers would be on the hook for $1.35 billion, according to an estimate by the college district. The levy is expected to be in place until 2049. The ballot language begins “Without increasing current tax rates,” then asks voters to authorize the bonds. “Of course it’s going to raise taxes. It’s just going to extend the debt for many more decades,” said Chris Robell of the Silicon Valley Taxpayers Association, which opposes the measure. The money would fund maintenance across all campuses, including upgrades to plumbing, electrical systems and roads, repairs for leaking pipes, and new computer lab equipment, according to the measure. The money would also be used to “reconstruct or modernize” two arts buildings, one at Skyline and one at Canada, and a library at College of San Mateo, per the measure. If the district secures matching state funds, Measure V bonds would also pay for new student housing at Canada College and Skyline College. Skyline College could get a new gym with a pool. Voters have approved at least $1.06 billion in bonds for the college district in the last 25 years. That money does not include the interest and fees associated with bonds. title: Bernice V. (Yoder) Alwine - Daily American
content: Bernice V. (Yoder) Alwine, 93, passed peacefully October 17, 2026 at her home. Born July 11, 1933 in Woodstown, daughter of the late Ammon and Elda (Kaufman) Yoder. Also preceded in death by husband of 69 years, Lowell T. Alwine on March 17, 2020; siblings Noah, Paul and Marlin Yoder and Dorothy Shetler, Twila Thomas and Erma Kauffman. Survived by son Gerald R. married to Jeanette (Replogle), Thomas Mills; daughter Louise K. married to Gary Hillegass, Thomas Mills; grandchildren Jennifer married to Daniel Miller, Matthew Alwine and wife Melanie, Alycia married to Timothy Blough and Jodi married to Timothy Mock; 16 great-grandchildren; sister Emma Mae Alwine; brother Merle Yoder and wife Janet; sister-in-law Doris Yoder and numerous nieces and nephews. Bernice was a lifetime member of Thomas Mennonite Church where she led singing, taught Sunday School and was a youth advisor. She also helped her husband on the farm and cleaned office for a local dentist. She then worked in the dietary department at the Allegheny Lutheran Home and then Laurel View Village. Along with her husband, she drove for Ernie’s Transport for the American Red Cross and delivered newspapers for the Johnstown Tribune-Democrat. Bernice enjoyed singing, solving wordsearch puzzles and reading her Bible. She especially enjoyed spending time with her grandchildren and great-grandchildren. She enjoyed life to the fullest, always joking and making people laugh. She would always take some Smarties candies to church and hand them to the kids and anyone who crossed paths with her. When asked how she was doing, she would reply, “Fine and dandy and sweet as candy.” The family would like to thank the staff of Meals on Wheels and Interim Hospice for the compassionate service and care given to Bernice. title: Liverpool v Villarreal: Where to Watch, Match Preview, Kick Off Time & More - Yahoo Sports
content: The start of three home games in a row for Liverpool sees them take on Villarreal in the Champions League. The Reds will be hoping that with the help of the Anfield faithful, they will be able to continue their perfect start to their European campaign. The last time these two sides met on Merseyside was during the knockout stages of the tournament back in 2022. A semi-final clash over two legs to decide who would go on to face Real Madrid in the final, held in Paris. The first leg was held at Anfield, with then Jurgen Klopp's side taking a 2-0 advantage over to Spain the following week. An own goal from ex-Brighton left back Estupinan, and a strike from Sadio Mane left the Yellow Submarine with it all to do to turn this tie around at home. LFC would advance into the final after edging out a five-goal thriller in Villarreal, before losing the final after Thibaut Courtois had a heroic game for the 15-time champions of Europe. A trip to the Gtech Community Stadium awaited Andoni Iraola's side over the weekend, a tough place to go, especially against a Brentford team that, up to that point, hadn't lost a game across all competitions. The first half showed the quality of the Bees, with them finally finding a breakthrough in the game thanks to a Keane Lewis-Potter header, giving Keith Andrews' side a deserved lead. Then a red card in additional time of the first half meant that the game was flipped on its head, with Liverpool now expected to be the side on the front foot trying to break down a stubborn and resolute Brentford defence. But the comeback would begin with a Victor Munoz goal, after Florian Wirtz slipped in the Spaniard on the right-hand side. Munoz then chopped inside and curled his shot, left-footed, into the bottom corner past Caoimhin Kelleher to equalise for the Reds. The turnaround would then be complete via a striker's finish from Alexander Isak, who marked his return to the matchday squad after sustaining an injury while away on international duty with Sweden, with a goal, giving Liverpool a 2-1 lead and eventually all three points. The Yellow Submarine have had a massive uptick in form in the last five games, going from a side that was struggling to stop losing, to now winning four of the last five. They have beaten European giants like Napoli during this period, and their only loss came narrowly to Real Madrid away from home. Under manager Inigo Perez, they will pose a tough test for Andoni Iraola's side, but the Reds will be confident that they can win this match and make it nine points out of nine. This match will kick-off at 8 pm (BST) and can be watched live in the UK on Prime Video. In the US, you can watch the game live on DAZN or Paramount+. title: 2028 Honda CR-V: The Coming Hybrid SUV That Could Haunt the Toyota RAV4’s Dreams - MotorTrend
content:
The next CR-V is a really big deal for Honda. Here’s what we expect from the next iteration of Honda’s bestselling compact SUV and what it may look like. No one expected the Honda CR-V to briefly become the bestselling vehicle in the country, but it happened earlier this year when the aging Honda was in the right place at the right time. That made us wonder: Could a new, redesigned CR-V grab the top spot among SUVs simply by being the best? We’ll soon find out when the new 2028 Honda CR-V debuts. Even before the 2028 CR-V arrives, reportedly sometime in early 2027, the outgoing five-seat compact SUV is already selling about as much as the Accord and Civic combined. It’s that big of a deal for Honda and the market as a whole. What you see here is our best guess at what the 2028 Honda CR-V could look like. Will Honda’s seventh-generation CR-V keep loyal buyers happy? Or will it be a regression from the outgoing SUV? Here’s what we believe we’ll see from Honda’s coming new compact SUV. The current CR-V is a solid compact SUV, but it’s no longer our favorite. Unlike the 2026 Toyota RAV4, which has gone all hybrid, the 2026–2027 CR-V still offers buyers a choice between gas and hybrid powertrains. To keep the price down, the lower trims are gas-powered, and the higher-priced trims are hybrids that generally include more features. For 2028, the CR-V is expected to go all-hybrid like the RAV4. We hope Honda will continue to offer a choice between FWD and AWD, if only to keep the base price down. We’ve already reported about how Honda’s new hybrid tech is said to be 30 percent less expensive to produce than before. That’s good considering the 2027 CR-V’s MSRP is already well above that of the Nissan Rogue, Kia Sportage, and Hyundai Tucson. The other major engineering change concerns the CR-V’s AWD system. The outgoing CR-V Hybrid uses a mechanical AWD setup, but the new model will be moving to an electric AWD approach. It’s a move that should help the 2028 CR-V better compete with the popular RAV4 in EPA-rated mileage and overall driving range. As for driving range, the RAV4 can achieve around 600 miles to a tank in a few configurations, an impressive number that the 2028 Honda CR-V Hybrid should come close to matching. We know Honda is developing its hybrid systems to be more efficient across a wider range of driving situations, which will likely mean higher highway mileage. Currently, the 2027 CR-V Hybrid sits at 40/34 mpg city/highway with AWD and 43/36 with FWD. RAV4 ratings vary by trim, but nearly every model is better than the CR-V. Perhaps not for long. The engine in the 2028 CR-V Hybrid could move to a version of Honda’s 1.5-liter turbocharged inline-four. The current hybrid uses a 2.0-liter naturally aspirated inline-four. We hope that if Honda moves to turbocharged power for the 2028 CR-V hybrid, it keeps an eye on driving smoothness. That may be just as important to some buyers as acceleration, though it must be said that the outgoing CR-V was slower in our testing than the model that came before. Honda’s Civic Hybrid offers a sublime driving experience (it uses a version of Honda’s naturally aspirated 2.0-liter at its core), so we’re crossing our fingers that the system in the new CR-V takes after that compact. Inside, the 2028 CR-V has work to do. Only a couple model years ago, Honda was still using an outdated 7.0-inch touchscreen on some CR-Vs. The outgoing model’s 9.0-inch display (pictured above) may make an appearance on lower trims, but we’re hoping the Accord’s 12.3-inch display is standard on most trims. Pairing that with the latest version of Honda’s adaptive cruise control and lane centering will go a long way toward making buyers think of the brand’s tech in a different way. Top-of-the-line 2028 CR-V Sport Tourings may also add Honda’s Sport+ feature that simulates shifts for a more connected driving experience, which debuted on the new Honda Prelude. We’ve tested it on the Prelude and haven’t been impressed so far. That trim level will be a greater value if it includes ventilated front seats and a 360 camera. Honda already offers these features in other markets on the outgoing model, so we know it’s possible. Part of what made CR-Vs so good in the past is the way they combine a spacious interior with a good driving experience and easy-to-use controls. The outgoing model was designed with physical knobs that made easy work of changing the temperature or turning down the air flow. Lately, some automakers have learned the hard way that touch-capacitive controls look tech-forward on a website but are difficult to use in person. Perhaps Honda can just skip to the part where it gives us controls that are simple to use. Another forbidden-fruit CR-V is the plug-in hybrid. Honda already offers one outside the U.S.; the real question is whether Honda will bring one here. A 2028 CR-V plug-in hybrid would allow Honda to compete directly with Toyota and its RAV4 PHEV, but it would add complexity to the lineup. Through September, PHEVs account for about 13 percent of all RAV4 sales in 2026. The 2028 CR-V should also return with a TrailSport model, though we hope this one has a more interesting interior than the outgoing SUV pictured above. Considering the Jeep Cherokee Trailhawk and Subaru Forester Wilderness, the 2028 CR-V TrailSport probably won’t be the most hardcore off-roader even within its segment, but it should offer an easier way for Honda’s more adventurous CR-V customers to head off the beaten track. Elsewhere in Honda’s lineup is the recently upgraded midsize 2027 Passport, and the Ridgeline truck returns soon, too. The truth is that unless Honda makes a steering wheel optional equipment or exclusively ships the CR-V in various shades of purple, the new 2028 model should be ubiquitous on American roads soon enough. Over time, though, that can change. That’s why it’s important that Honda doesn’t phone in the 2028 CR-V. Hyundai and Kia are making very good competing products, and the new Rogue Hybrid is one of the most impressive cars Nissan has made in years. In other words, buyers have choices. Whether the hybridized 2028 Honda CR-V remains among them will depend on how much new and improved stuff Honda adds to its bestselling SUV.
