title: Survey evidence from King Harald V’s funeral: those Norwegians who felt their grief was shared grew closer to the nation - Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO)
content:
Posted Monday, 19 Oct 2026 by Júlia Palik & Robert Jagiello We asked whether people felt more deeply connected to the nation before and after, and whether this made them more trusting and cooperative toward each other. This matters beyond the funeral itself. Norway’s preparedness strategy relies on a society whose members trust and help one another in a crisis. But how is that kind of social cohesion built, and what strengthens it? The funeral gave us a rare chance to find out. You can find more information about the survey at the end of the blogpost. Funerals are amongst the oldest and universally practiced rituals. They help individuals to process their grief and provide occasions for strengthening group ties in times of transition. Funerals have been empirically shown to influence people’s attitudes and behaviour: Participation in Queen Elizabeth’s funeral was associated with a visceral sense of oneness with a group, what social psychologists call identity fusion, a construct that predicts cohesion, trust, and sacrifice for a group. Another study found that mourners who endured more discomfort queuing to see Pope Francis's body gave more to a Catholic charity but not to a neutral one, showing that enduring the physically costly funeral ritual was associated with generosity toward one's own group. A study conducted in Kenya found that people who engaged in more traditional mourning rituals had more prosocial attitudes. Together, these studies suggest that funerals matter not only for individual grief but for group life. We set out to examine this by tracking how Norwegians' fusion, trust, and generosity changed around King Harald's funeral. In contrast to prior work, we surveyed the same people twice: before the funeral, on 3 September 2026 during the mourning period and on 10 September, the day after the funeral.Through YouGov, we reached 1,007 adults, weighted to be representative of Norway's population by age, gender, region and education, and 854 of them answered both surveys (1). Each time, we asked: The first survey also asked how much they admired the King, and the second asked how they followed the funeral: in person, live on TV or online, afterwards, or not at all. Because we heard from the same people before and after, we could track how each person's answers changed rather than just taking a snapshot. Since no one could be randomly assigned to watch the funeral or not, our findings show what goes together, not what causes what. We found that in the days after the King's death, before the funeral, many Norwegians already felt a visceral sense of oneness with the nation. This likely explains why the funeral did not raise it further on average. In our first survey, fielded during the mourning period, four in ten respondents chose the picture showing themselves entirely inside Norway. After the funeral, this was virtually unchanged (40% before, 39% after) (2). Because we have no measurement from before the King's death, we cannot say whether mourning raised fusion or whether it was this high all along. What we can say is that the funeral itself did not add to it on average. This matters: the study of Queen Elizabeth II's funeral found a similar link between shared grief and fusion but measured it only after the ceremony. Our before-and-after design shows the bond was already there beforehand, so funerals may be less a source of national bonds than events that enable the expression of such strong relations amongst individuals who do not know each other. What mattered for change in fusion was how people experienced their grief. Fusion rose among those who agreed that "people in Norway were united in grief with me," and among those who felt their pain was about the same as other Norwegians' (3). On average, respondents described their sadness as only slightly intense, and how sad someone felt during the funeral was not reliably linked to changes in fusion. Instead, grief, it seems, binds when it is felt to be shared. How people followed the funeral also made a difference. In the second wave we asked each person how they had followed it, live (in person, on TV, or online), only afterwards, or not at all, and we then compared their answers to the other questions across the two waves. Those who had watched live showed a larger increase in feeling united in grief than those who only caught up afterwards. Among live viewers, the share who were fully fused with Norway stayed about the same across the two waves (43% before the funeral, 44% after). Among those who did not watch live, it fell (34% before, 30% after). Live viewers chose to watch and were already more fused beforehand. We therefore see this as a promising lead rather than a firm conclusion: live participation may help hold the bond in place rather than create it. Before launching the study, we hypothesized that who dies matters for the outcomes we study. Admiration for the King was the strongest predictor (4) of fusion we measured before the funeral. It did not, however, determine who became more or less fused across the funeral: admirers were strongly fused before and stayed so after. Finally, fusion was not merely a private feeling but went hand in hand with how people saw their fellow citizens. Respondents whose fusion rose across the funeral also reported more trust in other Norwegians and a stronger sense that Norway is more united than divided (5). These links were modest, but they held when we used people's answers in the first survey to predict their answers in the second. These findings are striking in a country that already sits at the very top of European trust rankings, a pattern scholars call "Nordic exceptionalism". Even from that high a starting point, Norwegians who became more fused trusted one another more. People who felt more fused also said they would give more to a charity helping fellow Norwegians (6). However, how fused someone felt in the first survey did not predict their giving in the second, so this link is weaker than the one for trust. Taken together, the funeral did not further strengthen the national bond on average, most likely because the bond was already strong when we first measured it, after the King's death but before the funeral. Since we have no measure from before his death, this does not mean that the death and mourning left fusion unchanged. They may well have raised it, but our data cannot show this. What mattered for who grew closer to the nation was not the ceremony as such, nor the intensity of sadness, but the feeling of grieving together. This fits research showing that shared painful experiences, such as combat, terrorist attacks or natural disasters, can forge fusion even without a formal ritual. Because we surveyed the same people twice, our comparisons are made within each person, so stable differences between individuals, such as personality or political views, cannot explain the changes we see. And because we asked people both before and after the funeral, we avoid a classic chicken-and-egg problem: we can see that the funeral came first, and any shift in people’s views came afterwards.
This makes our design considerably stronger than a typical one-off survey, although events other than the funeral between the two waves could still have played a role. Measuring fusion is not a mere academic exercise. Fusion has crucial consequences for groups. A recent paper examining 90 studies shows that fusion predicts costly pro-group action, such as willingness to fight and die for the group, cooperation, or donation. As the opening paragraph of Norway’s Total Preparedness strategy states: “Norway is a long country, but we are bound by strong ties. We live across the length and breadth of the country and we have a fundamental trust in each other and in the authorities. This community of trust and good, safe and vibrant local communities throughout the country are the most important building blocks of Norwegian civil preparedness.” Identity fusion can be understood as a psychological building block of relations between humans. If relations are strong, people can effectively cooperate to achieve a goal, in this case the protection of the country. The strategy appears to treat trust and close social ties as given and constant, but they might change over time with potentially influential downstream effects. And while we detected no average change in fusion across the two waves, our data shows that more than four in ten respondents (373 of 854) placed themselves differently after the funeral. Those who moved into full fusion (87) were almost exactly balanced by those who moved out of it (94). In short, fusion can change over time, as shown by others too. Taking these psychological dynamics into account could make preparedness policy more attentive to how social ties are built and maintained, making the defense strategy truly people centered. We conducted a two-wave, within-person panel design. The same nationally weighted sample of Norwegian adults was surveyed twice through a YouGov omnibus: Wave 1 (N=1007) shortly before the funeral of King Harald V (fielded 3 September 2026; the funeral is on 9 September 2026) and Wave 2 shortly after (fielded 10 September 2026) recontacting the same respondents ( N=854). The funeral was a naturally occurring, non-repeatable event experienced by all respondents. The primary comparisons are within-person changes from Wave 1 to Wave 2, supplemented by moderation analyses using individual differences measured within the panel (e.g. attachment to the King, and mode of engagement with the funeral). The English and Norwegian versions of the questionnaire and our pre-registered design can be accessed through this link. All analyses presented here are preliminary. The final results will be reported in a forthcoming academic article.
We are grateful to PRIO’s leadership for providing funding for this study and enabling its implementation under extreme time pressure. Similarly, we would like to acknowledge the invaluable help of Per Ståle Ekrol and Jane Hansen for facilitating the inclusion of our survey questions into YouGov’s Omnibus. We further thank Henrikas Bartusevičius, Harvey Whitehouse, Ilze Gehe, Siri Aas Rustad, Michelle Delaney, and Haakon Gjerløw for providing feedback and support for our study. The authors

title: Jesse Eisenberg Says He 'Couldn't Get Movie Studio Parts' After Winning His Batman v. Superman Razzie - IGN
content: Jesse Eisenberg says he "couldn't get into studio movie parts" because he won a Worst Supporting Actor Razzie for playing Lex Luthor in Batman v. Superman. The Social Network star elaborated on what has become one of his most divisive roles when speaking at the BFI London Film Festival (via Variety). He recalled how his time as a long-haired Lex made landing acting roles more challenging, specifically calling attention to how his Golden Raspberry Award win played a part during a difficult time in his career. "Listen, a lot of it just came from fear," he said when describing his shift away from studio roles. "I couldn’t get into movie studio parts anymore because I had won a Raspberry Award from [being in the] Batman movie … and I saw the trajectory." Although the polarizing Batman v. Superman: Dawn of Justice does have its fair share of fans, Eisenberg's more eccentric performance as the Superman villain has remained one of its most controversial elements in the decade since its premiere. His acting was so…memorable that he walked away from the part with a Razzie for Worst Supporting Actor. Winning at the Golden Raspberry Awards, which recognize the worst components in movies each year, isn't usually treated as an honor. No one wants to be told they are the "worst" at anything, and having that Razzie label attached to your name can sometimes even secure a person's place in the hall of filmmaking infamy. Eisenberg said that's what his experience was after earning a Razzie for Batman v. Superman, and it's why movie fans didn't see him in as many big films in the years that followed. Instead, he learned to pivot to start writing and directing movies. Two projects to come out of that switch-up are 2024's A Real Pain and The Debut, which will premiere this December. "If you’re an actor, you’re constantly panicked about 'Am I on an upslope or a downslope?'" he said. "Because there’s no plateau. Acting is just this unstable, awful industry where you are either on the treadmill and you’re doing okay and you’re running up or you are yesterday’s news and it’s awful. And if you’re a paranoid person like me, you see it way in advance." Eisenberg continued: "The industry tells you what they want from you. The industry did not want me to be in a superhero movie, and if you’re smart and self-aware, you learn that quickly. And you know, it's the unsuccessful actor that goes 'No, I want to be in more of those.' It’s not going to happen and they don't want you there and they wouldn't have given you a Raspberry Award if they wanted you there. That's an award for bad acting. And so the industry tells you what it wants and if you want a career in the arts you have to follow the things that you’re being told are liked." Although the ex-Lex Luthor actor, who went on to reprise his role in Justice League, has found his footing in the years since his time in the DCEU, Batman v. Superman still has watchers split all these years later. IGN gave the film 6.8/10 review, saying, "BvS is carried by a brutal Batfleck, but as a whole it offers more philosophical drama than superhero escapism." title: Jesse Eisenberg Says He ‘Couldn’t Get Movie Studio Parts Anymore’ After Winning a Razzie for ‘Batman v Superman’: ‘The Industry Did Not Want Me to Be in a Superhero Movie’ - Variety
content:
Jesse Eisenberg has said he was frozen out of studio movies after winning a Razzie for Zack Snyder’s “Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice.” The Razzies — short for Golden Raspberry Awards — are a tongue-in-cheek ceremony that “honor” the supposedly worst films of the year. They are traditionally handed out the night before the Oscars. Eisenberg, who played arch villain Lex Luther opposite Henry Cavill and Ben Affleck, was allocated a worst supporting actor Razzie for his part in the 2016 superhero flick. Although supposedly lighthearted, the “award” damaged his acting career, Eisenberg admitted during a screen talk Sunday as part of the BFI London Film Festival, causing him to step back from acting and instead lean in to writing and directing. (Eisenberg’s latest directorial effort, “The Debut” starring Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti, is closing LFF Sunday night). “Listen, a lot of it just came from fear,” he said of his career pivot. “I couldn’t get into movie studio parts anymore because I had won a Raspberry Award from [being in the] ‘Batman’ movie … and I saw the trajectory.” “If you’re an actor, you’re constantly panicked about ‘Am I on an upslope or a downslope?’” he explained. “Because there’s no plateau. Acting is just this unstable, awful industry where you are either on the treadmill and you’re doing okay and you’re running up or you are yesterday’s news and it’s awful. And if you’re a paranoid person like me, you see it way in advance.” “So I was like, I’ve got to direct movies. That’s why I started writing them, just to kind of keep my career afloat, really.” “Batman v Superman,” which opened globally with an impressive $424.1 million box office, took home four Razzies overall, including for worst screenplay, worst sequel and worst screen combo for Cavill and Affleck. Eisenberg has previously said the film’s “poor” reception damaged his career. At the BFI talk, the actor said his takeaway from the experience was that he shouldn’t star in any more superhero films. “The industry tells you what they want from you,” Eisenberg said. “The industry did not want me to be in a superhero movie, and if you’re smart and self-aware, you learn that quickly. And you know, it’s the unsuccessful actor that goes ‘No, I want to be in more of those.’ It’s not going to happen and they don’t want you there and they wouldn’t have given you a Raspberry Award if they wanted you there. That’s an award for bad acting. And so the industry tells you what it wants and if you want a career in the arts you have to follow the things that you’re being told are liked.” One role the industry did want to see him reprise was that of Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg, given Eisenberg was nominated for a best actor Oscar for playing the tech titan in 2010’s “The Social Network,”  penned by Aaron Sorkin and directed by David Fincher. Despite that, the actor has been adamant he did not want to return in the recently-released follow-up “The Social Reckoning,” which Sorkin both wrote and directed. He didn’t expand on that decision during his LFF talk, other than to say the “companion movie,” as it has been dubbed, “is quite different.” He was more open about working with Kieran Culkin in Eisenberg’s sophomore directorial effort “A Real Pain,” which was released in 2024. The movie scored Eisenberg a nod for best screenplay and Culkin a best supporting actor win at last year’s Oscars, but the film could have turned out very differently. “We didn’t know if Kieran was ever going to show up to Poland,” Eisenberg revealed. “Emma Stone is producing the movie. She personally took him on the plane to Poland [where it was shooting] because we didn’t know if he was going to show up. She sent me a video of him going through customs, saying ‘We are here!’ and then he still was late.” And Culkin, who’d recently come off HBO’s mega-hit “Succession,” was adamant he wanted Eisenberg to use a similar “spontaneous” shooting style, which had not been part of the plan. “We’re like, what’s best for the movie?” the actor/director recalled as he tried to work out what to do. “And I guess what’s best for the movie is probably following this live wire around because that’s the engine of the movie anyway. If he had a small part, you’d be like, ‘We just have to tell this guy to shut up,’ you know? But he’s the lead… So it was a real learning curve.” 5 Comments Comments are moderated.
